extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funding-agency staff, and policy-makers concerned with grant peer review and gender equity
extracted.subtask_short: mitigating gender bias in grant review
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, implement, and evaluate interventions to prevent or reduce gender bias in the peer review of research grant applications (policies, reviewer training, anonymization, monitoring, and outcome measurement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-blinding (eliminating references to gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminating references to gender from the applications, letters of recommendations, and interview reports that were sent to the committee members for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented in an uncontrolled before-after study of EMBO Long-Term Fellowships (2006). The study removed gender references but provided lists of publications (which could reveal identity); reviewers could theoretically internet-search applicants. The study found no change in the proportion of successful applications led by women (14.7% post-intervention vs 14.8% pre), and the intervention was later discontinued. Recommendation: test gender-blinding using more rigorous designs and ensure de-identification is thorough (e.g., redact/reformat publication lists) to avoid re-identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate representation of men and women on peer review panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure appropriate representation of men and women on peer review panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as a strategy to mitigate gender bias. No direct empirical trial in grant peer review reported in this review; considered plausible based on equity principles. Implementation guidance: monitor panel composition and consider explicit targets or policies to diversify reviewer pools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training peer reviewers in unconscious/implicit bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide training or workshops to make peer reviewers aware of common biases and strategies to overcome them (implicit/unconscious bias training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: a 20-minute workshop changed participants' perceptions of bias; a 2.5-hour workshop (cluster RCT) increased self-efficacy to engage in gender-equity promoting behaviours and increased self-reported activity when ≥25% of department members attended. Suggested training elements include education on implicit biases, strategies for overcoming stereotyping, and tools like the Harvard Implicit Association Test. Recommendation: evaluate training via randomized trials for effectiveness in peer review contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure evaluation criteria are consistently applied (structured evaluations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured evaluations rather than unstructured evaluations to reduce bias and improve reliability/validity of assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sourced from literature on hiring and academic evaluations: structured scoring reduces subjective bias. Practical steps: define standardized criteria, use scoring rubrics, train reviewers on criteria application, and audit adherence. Intended effect: reduce variability and implicit bias in assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring equity across grant programs (collect/report gender statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish strategies to monitor equity across grant programs (e.g., track success rates by gender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH example: monitor equity across programs and public reporting (gender-disaggregated statistics). Use metrics such as success rates, award sizes, and career-stage stratified outcomes by gender. Regular monitoring can identify disparities and inform interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral wording in grant announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the wording in grant announcements to ensure gender neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH has implemented gender-neutral wording in announcements as a programmatic strategy. Impact is unclear because programmatic changes often coincide with other interventions; nevertheless, review and edit announcement language for gendered phrasing and implicit cues about ideal candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying funding to institutional gender-equity awards (e.g., Athena SWAN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make funding contingent on candidate organizations receiving gender-equity recognition (e.g., Athena SWAN Silver Award) to promote institutional-level gender equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK National Institute for Health Research required institutions to hold at least a Silver Athena SWAN award. Caveats: perceived heavy workload to meet requirements, and workload often borne by women, potentially reproducing inequity. Recommendation: consider unintended consequences and evaluate impact on grant success for women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous (double-blind) review without investigator identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct anonymous review of applicants without disclosing the investigator’s name or gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the one included EMBO study's gender-blinding was ineffective (possibly because publications could identify applicants), anonymous review has been effective in other domains (e.g., symphony orchestras, technology hiring, blind auditions). Recommendation: implement true double-blind processes where feasible and test with rigorous designs to assess impact in grant peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize language and descriptors in evaluations and letters of recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be self-aware and scrutinize the language and descriptors used to describe under-represented groups (e.g., differences in 'standout' adjectives in letters of recommendation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that letters of recommendation for men contain more standout adjectives (e.g., excellent, outstanding) which may influence outcomes. Practical guidance: provide examples of biased wording, train reviewers and letter writers to use balanced descriptors, and consider text-audit or linguistic review for systematic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend equal time on positive and negative aspects in peer review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure peer reviewers spend equal time discussing positive and negative aspects of an application when preparing reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested to reduce asymmetrical emphasis that may disadvantage certain applicants. Implementation: include explicit prompts in review forms (e.g., 'List strengths' and 'List weaknesses' with similar space/word limits) and audit reviews for balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measures for assessing gender bias interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure any outcome that assessed or measured gender bias (including awareness, knowledge, attitudes) or its potential impact (such as proportion of funded research projects by women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review defined eligible outcomes broadly: awareness, knowledge, attitudes, and concrete impacts like percent successful applicants by gender. Recommendation: use both proximal (attitudes, implicit bias scores) and distal (funding rates, award sizes) outcomes, disaggregated by career stage and field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of implicit-bias assessment tools (e.g., Harvard IAT) as part of reviewer interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include completion of implicit association tests (e.g., Harvard IAT) or online education about breaking gender stereotyping as components of reviewer training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended in conclusions as candidate interventions to be trialed. Guidance: pair self-assessment (IAT) with actionable strategies and follow-up training; evaluate changes in behaviour and downstream funding outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate interventions with rigorous study designs (randomised trials when possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test mitigation strategies using rigorous designs such as randomized trials to determine their true impact on peer review and funding outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend funding agencies support experimental studies (e.g., randomized trials of training strategies, anonymization procedures). Rationale: the scoping review found scarce and weak evidence (only one uncontrolled before-after study). Design guidance: include pre-specified metrics, adequate sample sizes, and measures to prevent re-identification in anonymization trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of de-identification limitations and re-identification risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that de-identification (e.g., removing gender references) can be undermined by information such as publication lists or internet searches and may therefore be ineffective if not comprehensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EMBO study noted publication lists were provided, allowing potential re-identification; reviewers may search online. Practical implication: if implementing anonymization, remove or mask identifying metadata (e.g., reformat publication lists, remove institution names where possible) and assess re-identification risk before roll-out.
